paragraphs.text: A useful way into these three chapters is to ask what each encounter lets you understand, and what remains outside it. A photograph offers a view; it cannot answer every question about the place or the people pictured. A performance can invite close attention without making its training visible. Begin with that difference between seeing something and knowing how it came to be.

Sangeet Natak Akademi’s 1991 citation records Chandra Sekhar Bhanj learning Mayurbhanj Chhau from his father, Bisweswara Bhanj, and other teachers. It also records his later teaching at the Chhau Training Centre in Baripada, on the invitation of the Orissa Sangeet Natak Akademi. This is a historical account of learning and teaching, not a notice of classes available today.

That account suggests a question to carry into the rhythm chapter: who taught the person whose work you are considering? If there is an opportunity to ask, let the answer name its own people and places. When watching, choose one transition to notice—an entrance, a pause or a change of direction—rather than trying to assign a story to every gesture. These are suggestions for attentive looking, not a lesson in interpreting Chhau.

Carry the same restraint into the forest and meal chapters. Separate what you notice from what you have verified, and leave unanswered questions visible in your notes. Treat the three chapters as different kinds of encounter, not a promise that a forest visit, a performance and a particular meal can be arranged together. The journey’s practical prompts remain the place to begin checking a plan.

notes.text: Sangeet Natak Akademi, Chandra Sekhar Bhanj, Akademi Awards 1991, p. 20.
